content.overview: BNS s. 72 — Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc. BNS restatement of IPC 228A. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 228A. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 72 is the rule on “Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc”. The section provides that (1) Whoever prints or publishes the name or any matter which may make known the identity of any person against whom an offence under section 64 or section 65 or section 66 or section 67 or section 68 or section 69 or section 70 or section 71 is alleged or found to have been committed (hereafter in this section referred to as the victim) shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 72 exists so that “Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc” has a closed legal test in Chapter V — Of Offences Against Woman and Child. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Sexual offences, assault, marriage, miscarriage, and offences against the child — placed first among the offence chapters.

The provision in detail
72. (1) Whoever prints or publishes the name or any matter which may make known the identity of any person against whom an offence under section 64 or section 65 or section 66 or section 67 or section 68 or section 69 or section 70 or section 71 is alleged or found to have been committed (hereafter in this section referred to as the victim) shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine

(2) Nothing in sub-section (1) extends to any printing or publication of the name or any matter which may make known the identity of the victim if such printing or publication is—

(a) by or under the order in writing of the officer-in-charge of the police station or the police officer making the investigation into such offence acting in good faith for the purposes of such investigation; or

(b) by, or with the authorisation in writing of, the victim; or

(c) where the victim is dead or a child or of unsound mind, by, or with the authorisation in writing of, the next of kin of the victim:

Essential ingredients
1. (1) Whoever prints or publishes the name or any matter which may make known the identity of any person against whom an offence under section 64 or section 65 or section 66 or section 67 or section 68 or section 69 or section 70 or section 71 is alleged or found to have been committed (hereafter in this section referred to as the victim) shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine
2. Subsection (2): Nothing in sub-section (1) extends to any printing or publication of the name or any matter which may make known the identity of the victim if such printing or publication is—
4. Clause (a): by or under the order in writing of the officer-in-charge of the police station or the police officer making the investigation into such offence acting in good faith for the purposes of such investigation; or
5. Clause (b): by, or with the authorisation in writing of, the victim; or
6. Clause (c): where the victim is dead or a child or of unsound mind, by, or with the authorisation in writing of, the next of kin of the victim:

Explanations
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, “recognised welfare institution or organisation” means a social welfare institution or organisation recognised in this behalf by the Central Government or the State Government

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Provided that no such authorisation shall be given by the next of kin to anybody other than the chairman or the secretary, by whatever name called, of any recognised welfare institution or organisation

Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:

learningObjectives: Understand the statutory prohibition on revealing the identity of sexual offence victims under BNS s. 72.
Analyze the scope of prohibited disclosure: print, electronic, and social media.
Examine statutory exceptions: authorization by victim, next-of-kin consent, or police officer in good faith.
State the punishment: up to two years imprisonment and fine.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 72 provides that whoever prints or publishes the name or any matter which may make known the identity of any person against whom an offence under section 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, or 71 is alleged or found to have been committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years and shall also be liable to fine. Exceptions permit disclosure under writing by the victim, police officer in good faith for investigation, or next-of-kin authorization to recognized welfare organizations.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Preserving the privacy, dignity, and social security of sexual assault survivors is a fundamental state interest. Public disclosure of a victim's identity subjects the survivor to secondary victimization and social ostracism, justifying strict criminal penalties.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 72 (corresponding to IPC s. 228A).
Protected class: Victims of offences under ss. 64 to 71.
Prohibited acts: Printing or publishing name, photograph, address, school/office, or any matter revealing identity.
Penalty: Imprisonment up to two years and fine.
Exception 1: Under order in writing by the police officer in charge of investigation in good faith.
Exception 2: By or with authorization in writing of the victim.
Exception 3: Where victim is deceased/minor/unsound mind, by written authorization of next-of-kin to recognized social welfare organization.
essentialIngredients: The victim is a person against whom an offence under ss. 64–71 is alleged or committed.
The accused printed, published, broadcast, or digitally circulated the name or identity-revealing details.
The disclosure was made without valid statutory authorization.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 72 strictly shields the identity of sexual assault survivors. The phrase 'any matter which may make known the identity' is interpreted broadly: publishing the victim's photograph with a pixelated face, mentioning her specific residential address, parents' names, or specific college roll number violates s. 72 if bystanders can deduce her identity. News media, digital portals, police officers, and private social media users are equally bound by this prohibition. In judicial judgments, trial and appellate courts anonymize the victim's name (e.g. 'Ms. X' or 'Victim A').
examples: Teaching example (Social media post): A news blogger posts the name and college address of a rape victim on a social media platform to gain views. Section 72 applies; the blogger is liable to two years imprisonment and fine.
Teaching example (Court judgment anonymization): A court judgment refers to the victim as 'Prosecutrix X' and redacts her home village to comply with s. 72 principles.
distinctions: Section 72 vs Section 73: Section 72 protects victim identity; Section 73 prohibits unauthorized publication of court proceedings conducted in camera.
General media freedom vs Protection of victim privacy: Freedom of the press under Art. 19(1)(a) is reasonably restricted under Art. 19(2) by s. 72 to protect survivor dignity.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a digital newspaper editor who published an article naming the deceased victim of a gang rape without next-of-kin consent is liable under BNS s. 72.
Rule: Section 72 prohibits publishing the identity of any victim of offences under ss. 64-71, extending to deceased victims unless authorized in writing by next-of-kin.
Application: The victim was named directly on the front page without any authorization from her parents or the police.
Conclusion: The editor is guilty of an offence under s. 72.
